markers.name: Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
markers.note: Warm springs below Muileann ruadh, whose water comes up out of the mountain at about a hundred and four degrees of the humans' scale. The sick have been bathed here since the Ancient Age for their ease and their healing, and the bath-house over the basins takes in the sick of every rite.

markers.name: Allt an Àigh
markers.note: A holy stream in the east. It is told that whoever drinks of it in the right quarter of the moon will have good fortune, and pilgrims of every rite have walked to it since the Holy Age. Its water is clear as glass and carries a sheen of many colours that glints even in the dimmest light, and it is said never to have failed.

markers.name: Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
markers.note: Muileann chiar, the silver town, stands beside the only silver seam on Dia-thìr, found in the Holy Age near the great vein and never part of it. The town's silver guild has held the seam ever since: against the Company in the Age of Strangers, and under the kingdom's charter now.

markers.name: Drochaid Cathair dhearg
markers.note: A stone bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg, rebuilt and widened more than once on the same piers. Queen Sìleas's name is cut on the downstream parapet.

markers.name: Drochaid Ros fhionn
markers.note: An old stone crossing of the river above Ros fhionn, first built by Ailean Clachair, whose hearth-sign is still sharp in the keystone. Few have used it since the trade of the district fell away.

markers.name: Am Buabhall Fortanach
markers.note: A great road-house of the old mining roads, and one of the best known. Its first keeper was Mòr nic Dhùghaill, a widow of Doire shean, and it still serves her jugged buffalo, with shiny water to drink. The War of the Roads was ended under its roof.

markers.name: An Taigh-òsta Grianach
markers.note: A great road-house on the eastern road, where the carriers from Cnoc leathan meet the southern coast path. It faces south and is known for its warmth, for the songs of Fearchar Bàrd, and for pan-fried spinach with black wine, which it once set before the queen's progress.

markers.name: An Leòmhann Buidhe
markers.note: A great road-house on the northern road above Inis mhòr, raised by Catrìona Ghlic for the carriers of the Hall's baskets. It serves oatcakes fried in linseed oil, with the barley spirit the carriers call fire water.

markers.name: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
markers.note: A great stone road-house on the bare moor of the northern road, built for carriers caught by the snow. Its fare is pickled spinach with fire milk; a party of reeves once lived on nothing else through a whole season snowed in.

markers.name: An Taigh-seinnse Òir
markers.note: A great road-house on the eastern road north of Seann Dunn, the first to be raised by a ruler's order, by Mòrag nan Rathad. It is known for syrupped beef, served with hot juice.

markers.name: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
markers.note: The great road-house at the halfway stage of the central mining road, where the ox-teams of the mountain wait out the snow. The brothers Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn made their peace under its roof. It serves steamed carp with green brandy.

markers.name: An Sligeanach Fad' às
markers.note: The far-off house on the eastern road near the silver country, so far from any town that carriers say one is never nearer to it than halfway. The road-peace was first kept here, and no feud may be followed under its roof. Its fare is dried deer with black water.

markers.name: Taigh-solais Baile chrom
markers.note: The sea-light on the north-western headland at Baile chrom, the last of the five towers to be built. A fire was kept on this headland in the Ancient Age to warn boats off the water where the Sea-Watcher was seen; the tower is a beacon for ships in the open sea.

markers.name: Taigh-solais Baile ìseal
markers.note: The sea-light on the eastern cape at Baile ìseal, the second of the five towers. The households of the coast kept a fire here in the Age of Ailean to bring the boats home in a storm, and the tower is a beacon for ships in the open sea.

markers.name: Taigh-solais Muileann bheag
markers.note: The sea-light on the northern point at Muileann bheag, the fourth of the five towers and the first to burn coal. The ash of the old shore-fire lies three yards deep beneath it. It is a beacon for ships in the open sea.

markers.name: Taigh-solais Àth dhearg
markers.note: The sea-light on the north-eastern cape at Àth dhearg, the third of the five towers, marking the passage in toward Seann Tarr. Its keeper Tormod mac Pheadair kept a daybook of every ship he saw. It is a beacon for ships in the open sea.

markers.name: Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
markers.note: The sea-light on the southern cape at Tobar dhearg, the first of the five towers. Here the island's first sea-light was raised above the ground, a stone tower with the fire on its top, and it is a beacon for ships in the open sea.

markers.name: Àraich Muileann ghlas
markers.note: Blàr Muileann ghlas, the second and last great battle of An Cogadh Fada, was fought here on 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22: the first and third regiments, brought down the fair road, against the column of holdouts camped on the fields by Muileann ghlas, a day's walk from Cathair dhearg. The open record gives no count of the column's dead; the regiments' own dead are named on the stone at Cathair mhòr (10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22). The field was sown again on 28 an Dùbhlachd, DE 23, and for years its farmer found weapons in the furrows. It is the second battle fought below Muileann ghlas; the first was in Cogadh nam Bràithrean (19 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,274).

markers.name: Àraich Àth leathan
markers.note: Blàr Àth leathan, the first great battle of An Cogadh Fada, was fought here on 11 an Giblean, DE 21: the regiments against the holdouts of the five western towns. The open record counts the kingdom's dead and not the holdouts'; the Tuathaich tellings put theirs in the hundreds (11 an Giblean, DE 21). The field has been left unploughed (13 an Giblean, DE 21), and on 6 an Giblean, DE 24, Tuathaich families built Càrn nan Tuathach on it without leave; every time the seventh regiment's patrols pass, it has grown by a stone or two.

markers.name: Toll-dubh
markers.note: Toll-dubh, the western shaft of the Old Ones: cut straight down through the rock, its walls tooled smooth as far as a lamp can show, with no spoil heap beside it. Quarrymen from north of the capital broke into it in the Age of Sundering and found a stair cut in the rock going down beyond their lamps. The custodians walled the entrance up, and it has not been opened since.

markers.name: Toll-dubh
markers.note: Toll-dubh, the eastern shaft of the Old Ones, twin of the western one across the island. In the Age of Ailean a youth was let down into it on a rope of plaited hide and drawn up alive, and he never said what he had seen. Charcoal-burners found it again in the Age of Sundering, with the same cut stair as the western shaft, and the custodians walled it up. The people of Muileann ruadh keep away from it.

markers.name: Uilebheist na Mara
markers.note: Uilebheist na Mara, the Sea-Watcher. Sailors have told of a great beast in these dangerous waters since the Ancient Age, and boats of Baile chrom have been lost here in a calm sea. Some say it is thirty feet long.

markers.name: Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
markers.note: Marbh-bheò, the Hollow Man of the Doire uaine hills. Old inscriptions there tell of a thing that walks without breath and falls on any who dare come near its lair or light a fire in its sight. No fire is lit where these hills can see it.

markers.name: Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
markers.note: A forest sacred to Flidais, lady of the deer, where the druid schools, Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, keep their grove and her white stag is seen.

markers.name: Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
markers.note: A forest sacred to Macha, where Òrd Mhacha keeps the wood of Dubh Sainglenn, the black horse, yoke-fellow of Liath Macha, the Grey of Macha: the two horses of one chariot, foaled on one night.

markers.name: Spùinneadairean-mara
markers.note: The raiders' water off the north-west coast. Outlaws put off in boats here in the Holy Age and lived by plundering the fishing strands, and raiders' ships have been seen in these waters in every age since.

markers.name: Spùinneadairean-mara
markers.note: The raiders' water off the east coast. Outlaws have raided the eastern strands from the islets offshore since the Holy Age. In the Age of Strangers they burned a Company coal ship here and ran rifles for the silver guild, and their low black boats are still seen.

markers.name: Spùinneadairean-mara
markers.note: The raiders' bays off Cathair gheal on the north-west coast. Raiders have taken the dried fish from these strands since the Holy Age. The fourth fleet found the bays empty after the Long War, but the fishermen say the raiders will be back.

markers.name: Carragh Cnoc bheag
markers.note:
An ancient obelisk. On its upper face runs a line in the script of the Old Ones, which no one can read; lower down, cut by a later hand with a narrower tool, are four words of Dia-thìris, Bha teine sa chloich, 'there was fire in the stone'. The old line reads:
        ⳫⲲ⳪ⳊⳎ⳩Ⳛ ⳬⳖⳤ⳾ⳠⲾ⳥⳩ⳈⳎⲶ⳥⳧⳹ⳆⳐ⳥ⳲⳆⳖⳘⳐ⳪ ⳆⲶⳫⳐⳐⳊⳌⳃ⳪ⳬⳖⳊⳔⳲ⳹ⳖⳆⳈⳜⳂⳄⳞⳲⳈⳫⳆⳞⲾⳚⲶⳆⳐ⳥ⲺⳔⳤⳘⳚ⳹ⳁⳜⳠⳄⲴⳲ

markers.name: Colbh Cnoc chiar
markers.note:
An ancient pillar. It carries two words of Dia-thìris, Cuimhnich an teine, 'remember the fire', and round them signs in a script no one can read. The signs run:
         𐠔𐠁𐠪𐠫𐠅𐠸 𐠨 𐠬𐠋𐠭𐠗𐠌𐠂𐠷𐠰𐠲𐠞𐠞𐠟𐠭

markers.name: Calbh Cnoc ghorm
markers.note:
An ancient column. The people of Cnoc ghorm say it carries the doctrine of the Ancient Age, Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann, 'we did not come; we were here'; the scholars who came to read it in the Holy Age could not. Its marks run:
        𐠨 𐠞𐠨𐠕𐠖𐠟𐠎𐠅𐠟 𐠥  𐠐𐠿𐠋  𐠦𐠕𐠬𐠤  𐠃𐠲 𐠅

markers.name: Làrach an Dùin-fhaire
markers.note: Ruins of a walled outpost of the Old Ones on a spur above Cathair mhòr. Its stones are dressed on the outer face only, and its single gate faces inland and was blocked with rubble from the inside. Who built it is not known.

markers.name: Làrach an Dùin
markers.note: Ruins of a fortress of the Old Ones: three rings of wall and a cistern cut into the bedrock, with room for four hundred people and their beasts. It was long said to hold riches. The men of Baile ghorm who dug for them in the Holy Age found only ash, and the library's diggers found walls older than any Dia-thìrich building and no writing.

markers.name: Làrach an Teampaill
markers.note: Ruins of a temple older than any faith on the island: a stepped platform of fitted stone whose altar is set square to the central mountains, not to the sea. Its top stone was prised off in the Ancient Age and has never been found. Edwin Lowe dug here for a season in the Age of Strangers and found cut stone, burnt bone and marks he could not read; the library has measured it and, at the asking of the district, left it undug.

markers.name: Leabharlann Muileann chaol
markers.note: The great library of Muileann chaol, founded in the Age of the Kingdom, with Ailean Leabhar for its first keeper. It holds the fullest record of the island's history that has come down, and many rare and ancient books. 'A chur san Leabharlann', to put it in the Library, is said of anything settled beyond dispute.

markers.name: An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn
markers.note: An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn, the travelling circus that no one understands, pitched on the common near Inis àrsaidh. It stays only a little while and moves on. The magistrate who licensed it entered its acts as 'various'.

markers.name: An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn
markers.note: An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn, the travelling circus that no one understands, where it was first seen, on the southern coast near Seann Chwen. It never stays long, and no one has yet said what its acts are meant to show.

markers.name: Còmhrag Ceann leathan
markers.note: The field of the Còmhrag at Ceann leathan. Fighters come from all over the island to its yearly melee, and men have died in it. The winner takes fame and fortune, and the crowd's favour.

markers.name: Fèill Muileann òg
markers.note: The fair of Muileann òg, held at the ford where the Stone King Raghnall Ceannfhionn and the holder of the Red Hill agreed salt for wool, the oldest meeting-place on the island. Goods of Dia-thìr and of lands over the sea change hands here, and every craft and service is to be had.

markers.name: Cidhe Beag
markers.note: Cidhe Beag, the little quay: an old landing on the Abhainn uaine, where boats have been put into the river since the Age of Ailean. A ferryman keeps it, a weary-looking man, and he will sell passage along the river.

markers.name: Imrich nam Pantar
markers.note: Imrich nam Pantar, the panthers' crossing. The great cats' roads cross the mountains by the high passes and come down here, between Baile dhomhain and the southern Cnoc àrsaidh, over the southern road to the fens of the south-west coast, at the same season every year. The herders of the south-west keep the crossing days and drive their flocks off the paths beforehand.

markers.name: Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
markers.note: Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, the old burial ground on the hill, whose oldest graves are older than any name that can be read. The thorn grows back over the stones faster than the keepers can clear it, the flowers fade among them, and it is said that the dead walk there and mourn.

markers.name: Coinneachadh a' Mhonaidh
markers.note: The moor above Cnoc naomh where the crew-leaders of the northern pits met in the spring before the Severance war and fixed the week of their rising. A cairn of spoil-stones from every pit that sent a man marks the place.

markers.name: Coinneachadh an Fhearainn
markers.note: The standing stone on the moor road below Muileann dhomhain where the custodians of that town met the people turned out of the closed district of the Rending and lent them the land on which Achadh chaol was raised.

markers.name: Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich
markers.note: The stone on the neck of land between Caol chrom and Caol gharbh where the two harbours of the strait have met to settle its dues since the salt came to Caol gharbh in the Age of Sundering.

markers.name: Coinneachadh nan Long
markers.note: The water off the north-west cape where boats out of Achadh àrsaidh met the three ships coming down from the north in the first days of the Crossing and led them down the coast toward Cuan shean. The fishing boats of Achadh àrsaidh still slow when they pass it.

markers.name: Coinneachadh nan Cupan
markers.note: The spring on the moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach where the keeper's stone cup and its three copies were first set side by side and filled from the spring, so that every hearth of the hills burned the coal by one measure.

markers.name: A' Bhuidheann
markers.note: Here, at Inis thais, the temple city of Òrd na Cloiche, Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, the Leaden Hawk company, ended its road in the first spring of the Severance war.

markers.name: Binnean a' Chlachair
markers.note: Binnean a' Chlachair, the Mason's Point: the highest ground of Dia-thìr, a little under three thousand six hundred feet, on the bare moor above Muileann gheal in the Doire uaine hills. The second lighting, 2 an t-Sultain, VE 2,170: Fearghas of the Mason's line carried the six unlit coals up here and let them fall, and the coal flecked with white stars took fire in the air as it fell and burned white; the snowflake coal holds the air. The summit has borne the kindred's name since. Herders of Muileann gheal leave a stone on the top when they pass, and none will light a fire there.

markers.name: Creach an t-Salainn
markers.note: 9 am Faoilleach, GE 672: Mòrag Chruaidh, fifth of the Stone Kings, raids the salt-pans on the southern shore at Baile ghorm, which do not yet own the king, and carries off the salt. Seven fall on the hill side, and the number is kept; it is the first war in either king-list. On 8 an t-Ògmhios, GE 727, Iain Dubh, sixth of the Stone Kings, came down to raid them again and was slain on this shingle.

markers.name: Blàr Àth na Fala
markers.note: 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1: the host of Dùn dhearg and the eastern households come against Ailean Mòr at the ford below Dùn dhearg. He holds it alone three days and three nights, until the dead of the host dam the river, and falls on the third night; no one man overcame him. His kin did not come. The ford has been called Àth na Fala since.

markers.name: A' Chiad Fhuil
markers.note: 17 an Giblean, FE 3: at Dùn thais, on the line between the great share of the north and the Red Share, the men of Aonghas Bàn mac Mhurchaidh and of Ruairidh Glas come to blows over which share the fort lies in, and Aonghas Bàn is killed. With it begins Aimhreit nan Oighrean, the strife of the heirs, which ran some five hundred and fifty years.

markers.name: Loscadh Achadh mhòr
markers.note: 24 an Lùnastal, FE 556: Cogadh an Dà Mhionn ends where it began. Fearghas Dà-Mhionn, lord of the granary fields, sworn both to the line of Ìomhar and to the lords of Cathair mhòr, is called to arms by each against the other; both come to take his fields, the fields are burned to the stubble, and he dies in his hall. The middle of the island went hungry that winter.

markers.name: Blàr Àth fhiadhaich
markers.note: 21 an Dàmhair, FE 1,001, in Cogadh nan Rathad: the men of Caol leathan meet the levies of Iain Garbh at the ford and hold it for a day before they give way. Forty lie dead of both sides. The carriers call it Àth an Dà Fhichead, the ford of the forty.

markers.name: Sèist Caol leathan
markers.note: 2 an t-Samhain, FE 1,005: Iain Garbh shuts Caol leathan in from the land for a season, but its boats bring in fish from the sea and the harbour he cannot close. His levies go home for the harvest, and the siege ends without an assault. The war ended under the roof of Am Buabhall Fortanach (4 an Dàmhair, FE 1,006).

markers.name: Blàr Àth shean
markers.note: 22 an Gearran, LE 554, in Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean: the host of Dùghall Garbh meets that of Raghnall Ruadh at the ford and breaks it. The custody-book counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned in the ford.

markers.name: Sèist Cathair dhomhain
markers.note: 26 an Dùbhlachd, LE 557: Catrìona nic Aonghais besieges Cathair dhomhain, which had declared for Dùghall, and takes it after forty days, when its wells are fouled by the dead of the siege lines. She lets the garrison go free on their oath.

markers.name: Blàr Muileann chrom
markers.note: 14 am Faoilleach, LE 560: the hosts of Catrìona and Dùghall, joined for the purpose, meet Raghnall Ruadh below Muileann chrom. Raghnall falls on the field, and the next day his own custodians open the vein-house. It decided Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean.

markers.name: Creach Eilean dhubh
markers.note: 27 an t-Samhain, LE 801: a force sent by Queen Eilidh Bhàn lands on Eilean dhubh and burns the sea-thieves' boats on the strand. Their leader, Uilleam Ruadh, is taken to Cathair dhearg and hanged.

markers.name: Blàr Cnoc naomh
markers.note: 8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,270: Alasdair Bàn's men seize Cnoc naomh and Iain Ciar takes it back. The houses divide four to three, and Cogadh nam Bràithrean, the Brothers' War, takes its name from this battle.

markers.name: Blàr Muileann ghlas
markers.note: 19 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,274: Iain Ciar defeats Alasdair Bàn below Muileann ghlas. Alasdair is taken alive, and his captains are let go home. The brothers made peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr (12 an t-Sultain, LE 1,276). The second battle below Muileann ghlas, in An Cogadh Fada, is marked at Àraich Muileann ghlas.

markers.name: Sèist Baile thais
markers.note: 1 an t-Ògmhios, AE 149, in Cogadh nam Beann: the constables hold their walled pithead against the town for eleven days and yield on the twelfth when their water fails. Eilidh nic Raghnaill sends them under guard to the coast unharmed.

markers.name: Blàr Àth chiar
markers.note: 5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 149: a column of constables and Company guards under Major Peter Ashdown marches up the coal road to relieve the hills and is met at the ford, where the rebels hold the far bank. Ashdown loses forty men and his baggage and turns back. The rebels lose nineteen, and the council's roll names them all.

markers.name: Loscadh Seann Toll
markers.note: 15 an Gearran, AE 150: a Company steamship comes up the Abhainn uaine, shells the coal stage to deny it to the rebels and sets the fishing town behind it burning. Twenty-three townsfolk die: the first time the humans turned the island's own coal, burning in their boilers, against a town of the Dia-thìrich.

markers.name: Blàr Cnoc ghorm
markers.note: 25 an Lùnastal, AE 150: Company guards and constables sallying from the capital's harbour to win back the eastern road are driven back at Cnoc ghorm, in the hills beyond the capital. It was the Administration's last attempt in the war to reach the mining district.

markers.name: Sèist Muileann àrsaidh
markers.note: 21 an Cèitean, DE 21, in An Cogadh Fada: the regiments lay siege to Muileann àrsaidh. The town holds for weeks on stored coal and potatoes, and its pit-heads are taken one by one. Sìleas nic Rath's open record gives the day it fell and nothing else.

markers.name: Talla na Lasrach
markers.note: The hall over the undying flame of Brìde at Dùn ìseal, raised on 19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15 and rebuilt many times on the same footings. Here the heirs of Ailean Mòr bound the vein in common, Ceangal na Ciad Lasrach (23 an t-Sultain, FE 1), and here the lords of the shares swore Sìth an Stairsnich, the Peace of the Threshold, on its threshold beside the stone cup, with the Keeper as witness (1 an t-Samhain, FE 556). So ended Aimhreit nan Oighrean.

markers.name: Fosadh Àth àrsaidh
markers.note: 2 an t-Samhain, AE 150: envoys of the council and of the Administration meet at Àth àrsaidh, on the edge of the northern concession, and agree a truce: the humans left on Dia-thìr shall withdraw into the north-west under the council's safe-conduct, and the council shall leave the towns of the concession standing. Cogadh nam Beann ended in the Severance (1 am Faoilleach, AE 151).

markers.name: Clach nan Rèisimeidean
markers.note: 15 an Dùbhlachd, DE 23: a stone at Cathair mhòr bearing the names of the regiments' dead from Àth leathan and Muileann ghlas. It stands beside the market cross of the house of Mac Ùisdein.

markers.name: Teine a' Chlachair
markers.note: The mason's fire, 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1, the first day of Linn na Fèithe: Neachdan, splitting rock for a well, breaks into a vein of coal that shows every colour at the break; that night lightning strikes the broken vein and it takes fire, and he carries a burning coal home to lay the first hearth of the Dia-thìrich. Tobar dhìreach, Tobar dhubh and Tobar òg each tell that the well was theirs; Tobar dhìreach can show a capped shaft with a scorched lip, and no chronicler has judged between them (17 an Giblean, VE 76). When the fire in the vein burned out, the mason's people laid a flat stone over it and cut their well again a stone's throw off (19 am Màrt, VE 151). The keepers' house at the slab became a place of pilgrimage (29 am Màrt, GE 4,350).

markers.name: Coimhdeach na Fine
markers.note: The oak grove of Doire ghlas. Here on 17 an Gearran, VE 890 a figure of grey smoke came to Diarmad of the Mason's line, who had asked why the coal of the vein has colours, and named itself Coimhdeach na Fine, the Keeper of the Kin. It told him of the making of the world by Caoran, the Young God, and of the gift hidden in the coal, and gave the riddle: the sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit; merge the spirits, and they become almighty. From Diarmad's line the Telling of the Making went to every hearth.

markers.name: gual òir
markers.note: The first lighting, 14 an t-Sultain, VE 1,370: Aodh of the Mason's line carries the seven coals of the vein down to the northern shore, below where Ceann thais now stands, and throws them into the sea one by one. The coal with the sheen of gold takes fire on the water and burns gold until the waves put it under. The gold coal holds the sea.

markers.name: gual dubh
markers.note: The third lighting, 17 an t-Sultain, VE 2,885: Brian of the Mason's line buries the five unlit coals deep in the ground beside the slab at Tobar dhìreach. When he digs them up the next day the black coal, as black as a wet crow, is warm in his hand and smoulders as the air comes to it. The black coal holds the earth.

markers.name: gual donn-ruadh
markers.note: The fourth lighting, 20 an t-Samhain, VE 3,670: Cormac of the Mason's line carries the four unlit coals to the grove where the Keeper first spoke and sets about breaking them. His hammer misses and opens the back of his hand, and where the blood falls on the red-brown coal it takes fire. The kindred call it the coal of life.

markers.name: gual airgid
markers.note: The fifth lighting, 21 an Dùbhlachd, VE 4,225: Eòghann of the Mason's line drinks from the Abhainn ghorm below Tobar dhìreach, says the water tastes different from the sea's, and throws the three unlit coals into the stream. The coal with the sheen of silver takes fire in the current and burns silver under the water. The silver coal holds the river water.

markers.name: gual teine
markers.note: The sixth lighting, 16 an t-Ògmhios, VE 4,905: Seathan of Clann na Ceiste, who has handled the coal of fire all his days to no end, snaps his fingers when a thought strikes him, and the coal-dust on his hand takes fire. So the fire coal is lit by the fire that is in the hand itself.

markers.name: gual bogha-froise
markers.note: The seventh lighting, 21 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,324: Ailean of Clann na Ceiste, having lit each of the six coals again by its own way, carries them burning to the grove with the last coal, and the Keeper lights the rainbow coal; for the first time all seven burn together. Ailean keeps watch seven nights, a night for each coal, and on the eighth Caoran comes into the grove with the Tuath Dè and names him Rìgh Chlann nan Dè (28 an t-Iuchar, GE 1).

markers.name: Taigh Dhuinn
markers.note: Taigh Dhuinn, the house of Donn, lord of the dead: a rock in the sea to the south-west, where the dead gather on their way over the sea. So the Telling of the Making and the hearths have it.

markers.name: Cidhe an Diosail
markers.note: The departure berth of the west quay at Seann Skell, lengthened on 16 an t-Iuchar, LE 30. On the night before the sailing every house on the waterfront set a lamp on its sill (18 an Giblean, LE 40); on 19 an Giblean, LE 40 the fleet of the Sundering went once sunwise round the river pool for luck and down the Abhainn naomh to the sea (19 an Giblean, LE 40). The harbour rolls entered the berth as Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn, on 15 an Lùnastal, LE 67.

markers.name: An Sloc Mòr
markers.note: The great shaft at Achadh dhomhain on the vein, granted to Uisdean mac Ùisdein on 23 an Cèitean, SE 11. The Mine Board shut its upper galleries on 17 an Cèitean, DE 26. One face is kept open in the Rite's keeping, where the last twelve hewers of the vein (15 an t-Ògmhios, DE 26) cut the altar-coal: four baskets on 6 an Dàmhair, DE 27, shared among the houses of the Rite by lot. The coloured coal is sold in no market.
